segments.original: With Star Wars (1977) and Superman (1978), audience interest in fantasy and science fiction films grew considerably, with Superman being the first major big-budget superhero film, performing well at the box office and with critics. The 1980s brought some successful adaptations, with RoboCop (1987) and Batman (1989), directed by Tim Burton (b. 1958), as the biggest highlights.

segments.original: In the early 2000s, the first Spider-Man was released in theaters, proving once and for all that films based on flamboyant comic book superheroes could work on the big screen. It is true that, two years earlier, the first X-Men had been released, receiving good reviews and a hefty box office. However, Bryan Singer's X-Men, good as it was, was still a work fairly removed from comic book aesthetics, without vibrant colors and colorful costumes.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The fear at the time was that this would not go over well with audiences, even considering the Superman films decades earlier. Spider-Man is a hero who, however much one might want to change his origin story and subsequent events, had to keep something crucial to his mystique: the costume. And we have to admit that the colors red and blue on a skintight suit covering the whole body, with web patterns and spiders on the chest and back, had every chance of not working on film. However, changing the costume, as Singer elegantly did in his X-Men, would have meant that fans (and Spider-Man has many, many generations of them) would stage an unprecedented revolt. It was no accident, then, that Spider-Man remained in so-called development hell for no less than 25 years.

tracks.title: Learn more: The Watershed in Superhero Films (2)

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Only when Sony, in 1999, bought the film adaptation rights from MGM, which had already commissioned a draft screenplay from James Cameron (b. 1954), did the film version of your friendly neighborhood Spider-Man really take off. Cameron was no longer attached to the project, but his work served as the basis for the screenplay that David Koepp (b. 1963) — writer of Mission: Impossible (1996) and Jurassic Park (1993), among many other famous films — ended up developing. Several directors were considered to helm the film, including Chris Columbus (b. 1958) and David Fincher (b. 1962). But it was when Sam Raimi joined the project that it began to take definitive shape. Raimi was firm about the film's structure, settling on just one villain, the Green Goblin, whereas the original idea was to use Doctor Octopus as well, in a secondary role. Likewise, with Raimi, the most dramatic change to the character's mythology would be made: the traditional mechanical web-shooters were replaced by controversial organic web-shooters, explained as part of the mutation Peter Parker undergoes after being bitten by a genetically altered spider. Spider-Man's suit was kept as close as possible to the original from the comics. It was given a rubbery look and raised webbing, and was molded to the actor's body almost as a single piece. Thus, the transposition from the pages of the comics to the screen was perfect.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Raimi, at the time best known for his work on the Evil Dead series, but who had also already made one of the best superhero films (though not one based on comics), Darkman (1990), was the perfect choice. His screenplay decisions were crucial to the film's success, and in addition he worked with a vibrant color palette, heavy on red, orange, and yellow, to keep the hero's and villain's costumes from standing out too much from their surroundings and also to mimic the multicolored comics of the House of Ideas. The result, for better or worse, was that the whole picture ended up with a strongly cartoonish feel, almost literally torn from the material that inspired it. The finishing touch was the essential work of veteran John Dykstra (b. 1947), famous for the special effects of Star Wars. The digital construction of the arachnid's movements may seem dated today, but that is only because technology advances at a maddening pace. The fact remains, however, that he managed to bring the hero's incredible leaps and acrobatics to the screen very effectively.

segments.original: Everything works very organically in the film, even though, of course, the time Raimi needs to tell the character's origin ends up taking away much of the picture's action potential. But the truth is that Raimi, along with Richard Donner (b. 1930) in 1978 and, more recently, Jon Favreau (b. 1966) in Iron Man, tells one of the best superhero "origin" stories, without ever letting the pace flag. It is a very well-balanced mix of respect for the original work, skillful adaptation, and balance with the rest of the film. Despite the bland performances of Dunst and Franco, Tobey Maguire's (b. 1975) Peter Parker — part goofball, part nerd, part beloved nephew, but entirely hero — has a perfectly acceptable arc throughout the film. Willem Dafoe (b. 1955) plays the comics' cartoonish villain just as the role demands, serving as a counterpoint to Parker's more serene attitude. The production design's sin lies in the, shall we say, Power Rangers-style armor the Goblin was given, but it does not compromise the result. Spider-Man remains one of the best examples of a great superhero film. At the very least, the film deserves its status as a watershed for the genre.

segments.original: The Crow (1994), directed by Alex Proyas (b. 1963), ended up becoming a pioneer in the evolution of the adaptations that would follow its release, with a darker and more violent story aimed at a more mature audience. The success of The Crow spurred the release of a film version of Spawn (1997), the flagship character of Image Comics. The success of Image Comics' "darker" characters changed the direction of comic book films.

segments.original: In 2002, the Spider-Man phenomenon hit theaters, breaking box office and DVD sales records. Its success followed a long list of uneven adaptations of Marvel and DC heroes, such as Daredevil (2003), Hulk (2003), Catwoman (2004), Hellboy (2004), and Fantastic Four (2005). Some critics and experts attributed the rising popularity of superhero franchises to the social and political climate in Western society since the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, while others argued that advances in special effects technology played a more significant role.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Even with all the success enjoyed by the competition, few films have reached the excellence of The Dark Knight – in quality and in numbers. It was the first comic book hero adaptation to break the $1 billion barrier at the box office. It earned an Oscar for one of its leads, Heath Ledger, who delivered the best version of the Joker in any medium. It established a tone and a narrative style that brought fantasy characters into the "real world" in a believable way. Perhaps only Logan (2017), among screen superhero films, has achieved such thematic depth and such dramatic density.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Nolan obviously had no interest whatsoever in getting his hands on other heroes from the DC catalog. The idea of a "shared universe," of using one film as just another brick to complete a wall, never crossed his mind. His trilogy made it clear that his interest was, rather, in creating an allegory about the darkest corners of the human mind, such as fear, obsession, revenge, and madness. Batman and the characters orbiting his adventures proved to be the perfect starting point for exploring very real themes. A perfect approach, which turned the director's second film with the Caped Crusader into a worldwide phenomenon, legitimizing "superhero movies" as a force to be reckoned with beyond box office numbers.

Perhaps that is the best legacy of the adventure that pitted Christian Bale (b. 1974) and Heath Ledger against each other in a duel that was less physical and more psychological: it is never too late to learn new tricks.
